::: {.lead}
The chests of *Torch Hall* give items of four rarities: common, rare, epic and
legendary. If every rarity had the same chance, a legendary sword would drop
in every fourth chest, and nobody would be excited about it. The damage of a
hit should vary, but not jump between 1 and 18. And the coins in the round
treasure room all lie in the middle. In lecture 22 you learned how a game
makes random numbers. In this lesson you learn to **shape** them: a
**uniform** distribution, a **weighted** choice with a loot table, a
**bell** shape from sums, and an even spread over an area. Every section ends
with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary probability-distribution uniform-distribution weighted-random weight cumulative-weight loot-table histogram bell-curve random-variable >}}

## 23.1 Distributions and histograms

A random variable can take many values. Its **distribution** says how
likely each value is.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 23.1 — Distribution and histogram"}
The **probability distribution** of a random variable lists every value with
its probability; the probabilities add up to 1. A **histogram** shows how
often each value came in many tries; with many tries it looks like the
distribution (lecture 20).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 23.1 — Two distributions"}
1. One die: values 1 … 6, each with probability 1/6.
2. A chest: common 0.6, rare 0.3, epic 0.09, legendary 0.01. Sum: 1.
3. After 1000 chests the histogram shows about 600, 300, 90 and 10.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Judging a distribution from 20 tries. Small samples jump a lot; use hundreds
or thousands of tries before you decide that something is wrong.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Write a distribution"}
Write the distribution of "the number of heads with two coins" (0, 1 or 2)
as a table of values and probabilities. Check that the sum is 1.

*Your result:* a table with three rows.
:::

## 23.2 The uniform distribution

The simplest distribution gives every value the same chance (@fig-uniform).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 23.2 — Uniform distribution"}
In a **uniform distribution** every value is equally likely. **Discrete:** n
values, each with probability 1/n (`Random.Range(0, n)`). **Continuous:**
every number in a range is equally likely (`Random.Range(0f, 10f)`); the
chance to land in a part of the range is proportional to its length.
:::

![A uniform distribution.](images/uniform.png){#fig-uniform width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 23.2 — A random spawn time"}
A bat appears after `Random.Range(2f, 6f)` seconds. P(the bat comes in the
first second of the range, from 2 to 3) = 1/4, because 1 s is a quarter of the
4-second range.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using a uniform choice when the design wants rare items. With four rarities,
uniform means 25 % legendary: rarity needs weights.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Uniform chances"}
(a) `Random.Range(0, 8)`: P(5)? (b) `Random.Range(0f, 10f)`: P(the value is
from 7 to 10)? (c) Why is P(exactly 7.000…) zero in (b)?

*Your result:* three answers.
:::

## 23.3 Weighted random choice

Most loot in games is **weighted**: each option has a weight, and heavier
options come more often (@fig-weighted).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 23.3 — Weighted choice"}
Each option i has a **weight** wᵢ ≥ 0. Its probability is
$$P(i) = \frac{w_i}{w_1 + w_2 + \dots + w_n}.$$
To pick: compute the **cumulative weights**, draw r uniformly from 0 to the
sum, and take the first option whose cumulative weight is greater than r. A
**loot table** is such a list of items and weights.
:::

![Weighted choice with cumulative weights.](images/weighted.png){#fig-weighted width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 23.3 — A chest of Torch Hall"}
Weights 60, 30, 9, 1 (sum 100); cumulative 60, 90, 99, 100.

1. r = 72: the first cumulative value above 72 is 90 → **rare**.
2. r = 99.4: above 99 → **legendary** (the bar from 99 to 100).
3. P(epic) = 9/100. With weights 3 and 1, P = 3/4 and 1/4: the sum does not
   need to be 100.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
int PickWeighted(int[] w) {
    int sum = 0; foreach (int x in w) sum += x;
    float r = Random.value * sum;          // 0 … sum
    int acc = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < w.Length; i++) {
        acc += w[i];
        if (r < acc) return i;             // first cumulative value above r
    }
    for (int i = w.Length - 1; i >= 0; i--)
        if (w[i] > 0) return i;            // r == sum (Random.value can be 1)
    return -1;                             // all weights are 0
}
```
:::

{{< sim file="sims/loot-table-lab.html" poster="sims/loot-table-lab.png" title="Loot Table Lab: weights and chances" height="740" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using `r <= acc` with a weight of 0: an item with weight 0 can then drop when
r lands exactly on its border. Use `r < acc`, so weight 0 means "never".
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A loot table"}
1. In **Loot Table Lab**, open 1000 chests and compare the counts.
2. Make epic items 5 % of the drops, and write your weights.

*Your result:* a count and a set of weights.
:::

## 23.4 Bell shapes from sums

Adding random numbers changes the shape: the middle becomes common
(@fig-sums).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 23.4 — Sums of random numbers"}
The sum of several uniform random numbers is **bell-shaped**: values near
the middle can be made in many ways, extreme values in few. The more numbers
you add, the stronger the bell. Games use it for damage, stats and
"natural" variation.
:::

![Sums of dice.](images/dice-sums.png){#fig-sums width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 23.4 — Damage 3 … 18"}
1. `Random.Range(3, 19)`: uniform, P(3) = P(18) = P(10) = 1/16.
2. Three dice: P(3) = 1/216, but P(10) = 27/216 ≈ 12.5 %.
3. Both have the same range, but the dice make damage steadier and extreme
   hits rare and exciting.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"One die × 3 is the same as three dice." One die × 3 gives only 3, 6, 9, …,
18, all equally likely: still uniform, with gaps.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Shapes"}
In **Distribution Shape Lab**, compare damage from 1 die and from 3 dice.
Write the most common values of each.

*Your result:* two answers.
:::

## 23.5 Random points in an area

Spawning coins or enemies at random places is a uniform choice over an
**area**, not over a number (@fig-circle).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 23.5 — Uniform in an area"}
- In a rectangle: x = Random.Range(xmin, xmax), y = Random.Range(ymin, ymax).
- In a circle of radius R: angle a = 2π · Random.value and
  **radius = R · √(Random.value)**. The square root is needed because the
  outer rings have more area than the inner ones.
:::

![Random points in a circle.](images/circle-points.png){#fig-circle width=94%}

{{< sim file="sims/shape-lab.html" poster="sims/shape-lab.png" title="Distribution Shape Lab: flat, bell or crowded?" height="700" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 23.5 — The round treasure room"}
1. With radius = R · r, half of the coins land in the inner circle of radius
   R/2, which has only a quarter of the area.
2. With radius = R · √r: the inner circle gets about a quarter of the coins,
   as it should.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Picking x and y in the square around the circle and keeping all points: some
land outside the room. Either throw those away and pick again, or use the
angle and √r.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The round room"}
In **Distribution Shape Lab**, scatter 1000 coins both ways. How many land in
the inner half of the radius each time?

*Your result:* two counts.
:::

## Case study: Loot Forge

The loot designer of *Torch Hall* has six questions: the chance of an epic
item, weights that do not add up to 100, which item a cumulative r picks,
steady damage from 3 to 18, coins crowded in the centre of the round room,
and an item with weight 0. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses
these questions. In the mini-game below you answer them.

{{< sim file="sims/loot-forge.html" poster="sims/loot-forge.png" title="Loot Forge: shape the randomness" kind="game" height="440" >}}

## Further reading

Rabin (ed.), *Game AI Pro* (2013), Chapter 3 "Advanced Randomness Techniques
for Game AI". Rosen, *Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications*, 8th ed.,
Section 7.4.

## Exercises

1. What must the probabilities of a distribution add up to?
2. Random.Range(0, 5) with integers: P(3)?
3. Random.Range(0f, 20f): P(the value is less than 5)?
4. Weights 5, 3, 2: the three probabilities?
5. Weights 2 and 6: P(the first option)?
6. Cumulative weights 50, 80, 95, 100 and r = 81: which option?
7. Which weight makes an option impossible?
8. How do you make a legendary item 1 in 200 with weights?
9. Why is the sum of two dice not uniform?
10. Three dice: P(sum 3)?
11. Why is one die × 3 not the same as three dice?
12. Write the two lines for a random point in a rectangle 0 … 10 by 0 … 6.
13. Why does a random point in a circle need √r?
14. In a circle with radius = R · r, which part gets too many points?
15. A designer wants enemy health around 100, rarely below 80 or above 120.
    Uniform or a sum? Why?
16. Write P(i) for a weighted choice as a formula.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. 1.
2. 1/5.
3. 5/20 = 1/4.
4. 5/10, 3/10, 2/10.
5. 2/8 = 1/4.
6. The third option (80 ≤ 81 < 95).
7. 0.
8. For example weight 1 with a total of 200.
9. The middle sums can be made in more ways.
10. 1/216.
11. It gives only multiples of 3, all equally likely.
12. x = Random.Range(0f, 10f); y = Random.Range(0f, 6f).
13. The outer rings have more area and need more points.
14. The centre.
15. A sum: it is bell-shaped, so values near 100 are common and far values
    rare.
16. P(i) = wᵢ / (w₁ + … + wₙ).
:::
